newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: DMG sees pick-up in Singapore exports in Q2 1997.
newsitem.headline: DMG sees pick-up in Singapore exports in Q2 1997.

text.p: Singapore's slump in exports is bottoming out and figures for the second quarter of the year should show a recovery, investment bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) said on Thursday.

DMG said in its bi-monthly review of Asian economies that recent reports units of the Royal Dutch/Shell Group, Mobil Corp and Seagate were planning to cut production in Singapore had introduced uncertainty into the export picture for the city-state.

"However, excess pessimism should be avoided. The current problem is essentially cyclical rather than structural. The question is not whether the recovery will come, but when and how strong," the report said.
"It is our judgment that the export sector is at or near its cyclical trough and each passing month brings it closer to the point of recovery."
Singapore is heavily dependent on electronics and related products, which account for about half its industrial production and almost 60 percent of its non-oil exports.
A slump in world electronics orders last year plunged Singapore's export sector heavily into the red for the first time in a decade.
Non-oil exports contracted by two to three percent year-on-year in the second half of 1996 and by 4.1 percent in the first quarter of 1997.
But DMG said manufacturers were already more upbeat about Singapore's prospects and noted net investment commitments had risen 66 percent in the first quarter of this year.
"Expectations of new manufacturing orders indicate that non-oil domestic exports could expand by 6.0 percent in the second quarter," it said.

"While we still maintain that this year's non-oil domestic export growth will be disappointing relative to expectations, the momentum in the coming months will put the economy on good ground for a full upswing into 1998."
It restated its previous forecast that the Singapore economy would expand by around 6.2 percent in 1997 and by 7.5 percent next year.
DMG said Singapore's measure of narrow money, M1 -- notes and coins in circulation -- might rise as the recovery gained pace, but gave no specific forecast.
It said loans growth could slow to 10-11 percent at the end of this year or early in 1998, compared with a peak around 20 percent at the end of 1996.
This could put pressure on banks and other lending institutions, ensuring that three-month interbank interest rates stayed close to the current 3.4 percent for the next few months.
The Singapore dollar was expected to rise gradually from its current level at around 1.43 to the U.S. dollar to around 1.41 in six months' time and to around 1.39 in 12 months.
